Emulator InternalsZX81: How the Screen Is Drawn

ZX81: How the Screen Is Drawn

Most home computers have a video chip that reads screen memory by itself while the CPU gets on with its work. The ZX81 has none. Sinclair built it to a price, and its picture is made by a clever partnership: the Z80 CPU walks through the screen memory as if it were a program, and a small custom chip, the ULA, catches each byte on the way past and turns it into dots on the television.

This article explains how that works, step by step. You need to know the Z80 (registers, opcodes, interrupts) and have some engineering basics. You do not need to know anything about televisions or video hardware: we start there.

Be prepared for something remarkable. The ZX81’s picture is not the work of one clever trick but of a whole orchestra of hardware and software playing in time: the ULA’s counters and sync pulses, two kinds of interrupt, a register used as a countdown timer, the CPU’s own refresh cycles, and a handful of ROM routines that hand the CPU back and forth twice a frame, all timed to the single T-state. Each piece is simple on its own. What makes it sophisticated is how precisely they fit together, and some of the most elegant details only show once you see the whole. So this is an article to read carefully, and in order.

How this article is organised

The parts build on each other, from the general idea to the finest detail:

  • The foundations: how a television draws a picture and why timing is everything (Part 1), the chips and interrupt signals involved (Part 2), and how the screen is stored in memory (Part 3).
  • The central idea (Part 4): the CPU executes the screen, then a whole frame at a glance, with the routine that runs it and the endless loop your programs run inside. If you read only one part, read this one.
  • The text and the borders (Part 5 and Part 6): how the text is drawn, every line exactly 207 T-states long, and how the borders are made. These parts carry the real ROM code, with every instruction explained.
  • Sharing the CPU (Part 7): how your program and the display take turns on one Z80. In SLOW mode they are two tasks, switched four times a frame; in FAST mode the display is a subroutine the ROM calls while it waits for a key. The part ends with the rules your programs must follow.
  • Three stories built on the same machinery: a keyboard routine that never varies by a T-state (Part 8), high-resolution graphics (Part 9), and the 64K ZX81 (Part 10).
  • The emulator (Part 11): how Klive reproduces all of this, and where to read its code. A table of all the display routines and a Summary close the article.

Each part gives you the gist first and then the details. On a first reading you can follow the gist and skim the listings; on a second, the listings show you exactly how it is done. Every complete ROM listing here assembles to exactly the bytes in the real ROM, and the timings were checked on Klive’s emulator.

Everything below is how the real machine works and how Klive emulates it. Klive’s ZX81 core does not “read the screen memory and draw text”: it runs the ROM’s own display code on its Z80 and lets its ULA react to every bus cycle, exactly as the hardware does. The last part shows where each piece lives in the source.

Part 1: How an old television draws a picture

The electron beam

A cathode ray tube (CRT) television has an electron gun at the back of the glass. It shoots a thin beam of electrons at the inside of the screen, which is coated with phosphor: wherever the beam hits, the phosphor glows for a moment. A stronger beam makes a brighter dot; no beam leaves the spot dark.

The beam can light only one spot at a time. To make a whole picture, magnetic coils around the tube sweep it across the screen in a fixed pattern called a raster:

  1. The beam travels from left to right, drawing one horizontal scan line.
  2. At the right edge it snaps back to the left, a little lower, and draws the next line. This quick return is the horizontal retrace.
  3. When it reaches the bottom, it snaps back to the top-left corner and starts again. This is the vertical retrace.

A European (PAL) television draws a line every 64 microseconds and a full screen, a frame, 50 times a second. That is fast enough that your eye sees a steady picture instead of a moving dot.

The signal carries only “how bright, right now”

Here is the part that matters most. The signal going into the television does not contain pixels or coordinates. It is just one voltage that changes over time, and it means “this is how bright the spot under the beam is, at this very instant”.

The television does not know which dot belongs where. It knows only when. A dot appears 20 microseconds into a line because the voltage changed 20 microseconds after the line started. In a video signal, time is position.

So how does the television know when a line or a frame starts? The signal also carries two kinds of special pulses, each a short stretch of “blacker than black” voltage:

  • HSYNC (horizontal sync): “start a new line now”. One arrives every 64 µs.
  • VSYNC (vertical sync): “go back to the top now”. One arrives every frame. It is much longer than an HSYNC, so the television can tell them apart.

The ZX81 needs only the three levels of the diagram, because its dots are either black or white. In Wilf Rigter’s description of the ZX81 video hardware , the ULA’s video output sits at about +5 V for white, +2.5 V for black and 0 V for sync. A resistor divider then scales these down to about +1 V, +0.5 V and 0 V at the input of the TV modulator. The same source gives HSYNC as about 5 µs long, every 64 µs, and VSYNC as about 400 µs long. These are nominal figures: owners who have measured their machines report noticeably different levels, which vary with the board and the ULA version.

The television locks onto these pulses. Its own sweep circuits (the flywheels) keep running at roughly the right speed even if a pulse is missing, which is why a picture rolls or tears rather than vanishing when the sync goes wrong.

Why you must follow the beam

There is no memory inside an old television. Nothing stores the picture. Whatever is on the signal wire now becomes the dot under the beam now, and a few milliseconds later it has faded away. So the computer has to deliver every dot at exactly the right microsecond, 50 times a second, forever. Programmers call this racing the beam.

PAL and NTSC. “50 times a second” is the European PAL standard: a line every 64 µs and 50 pictures a second, with 625 lines split into two interlaced halves of 312½. North America and Japan use NTSC: about 60 pictures a second, with 525 lines in halves of 262½. Home computers like the ZX81 ignore the interlacing and simply draw the same half-frame every time.

The ZX81 handles both with the same 207 T-state line, which fits either standard. The US machine (sold as the Timex Sinclair 1000) only draws fewer border lines: 263 lines a frame, about 60 frames a second, against 311 lines and about 50 on a European machine. The ROM finds out which kind of machine it is on by itself (Part 8 shows how). This article gives the PAL numbers unless it says otherwise.

That is why an accurate emulator also has to keep a virtual beam: a model of where the real beam would be at every moment of the emulated machine’s time. If a program changes something halfway down the screen, the emulator must show the change from that line onwards, not on the whole picture. On the ZX81 this is not an optional extra, because, as you will see, the picture is nothing but the CPU’s timing turned into light.

Part 2: The players

The ZX81 has very few chips, and three of them make the picture. Two interrupt signals tie them together, and they are players just as much:

PlayerIts job in the picture
Z80 CPU, 3.25 MHzRuns the ROM’s display routines, and walks through the screen memory one byte per instruction.
ULA (Uncommitted Logic Array)Sinclair’s custom chip. Makes HSYNC every 207 T-states all by itself (except during VSYNC), and VSYNC when the ROM asks for it. Counts scan lines, intercepts bytes on the data bus and turns them into dots, and shows white wherever there is nothing to draw.
8K ROMHolds the display routines and the character set: 64 characters of 8 × 8 dots at $1E00–$1FFF.
INT, the Z80’s maskable interruptWired to address line A6 (Part 5 shows the trick). Used only while the text is drawn, as its metronome: it ends each scan line of text at exactly the right moment and starts the next one.
NMI, the Z80’s non-maskable interruptRaised by the ULA at the start of each HSYNC, but only in SLOW mode and only during the borders. It counts the blank lines while your program runs, and with the last one takes the CPU back for the display (Part 6).

The RAM holds the display file (what is on the screen), but the RAM itself does nothing special.

Three numbers that make it all fit

Everything in the ZX81’s video design hangs on a few lucky numbers. Keep these in mind:

  • The Z80 runs at 3.25 MHz, so one clock cycle (a T-state) lasts about 0.31 µs.
  • One scan line is 207 T-states: 207 × 0.31 µs ≈ 64 µs, one PAL line.
  • The ULA puts out dots at 6.5 MHz, so it draws 2 dots per T-state.

From the last one: a character is 8 dots wide, so it takes 4 T-states to draw. And 4 T-states is exactly the time a Z80 needs to execute a NOP. That coincidence is the whole design. Hold on to it.

Registers that belong to the display

Because the CPU draws the picture, some of its registers belong to the display, not to your program: machine code on the ZX81 must leave them alone. Which ones, and why, only makes sense once you have seen how the display uses the CPU, so the full list comes at the end of Part 7, under Rules for your programs.

Part 3: The display file

The screen is 24 lines of 32 characters, 256 × 192 dots. Its contents live in RAM in the display file, whose address the system variable D_FILE (at $400C) holds:

  • It begins with a NEWLINE byte ($76).
  • Then come the 24 lines. Each one is its characters, one byte each, followed by another $76.
  • With 16K of RAM every line has its full 32 characters. On a 1K machine the ROM saves memory by collapsing the display: a line holds only the characters up to its last non-space one, and an empty line is just its $76.

Inside a character byte

Each character byte is a character code, and its bits have three different jobs:

BitsNameMeaning
0–5Character indexWhich of the 64 characters, 0–63. The shape of character n is the 8 bytes at $1E00 + n × 8 in the ROM.
6“Not a character”Always 0 in a character. A code with bit 6 set is not something to draw.
7Invert0: black on white. 1: the same character inverted, white on black.

Bits 0–5 pick the shape. The ZX81 does not use ASCII: $00 is a space, $1C–$25 are the digits 0–9, and $26–$3F are the letters A–Z. In between are a few block graphics and punctuation marks. There are no lower-case letters.

Bit 7 is the simplest: $2D is H, $AD is an inverted H. Altogether, the codes you can draw are $00–$3F and $80–$BF.

Bit 6 is the special one. It is 0 in every drawable code, so codes with it set ($40–$7F and $C0–$FF) can never appear on the screen as characters. The ZX81 uses them for other things, such as BASIC keywords and control codes, and one of them has a job in the display file itself: the NEWLINE code that ends every line, $76. That gives the hardware an easy test. A byte with bit 6 clear is a character to draw; a byte with bit 6 set is not. Part 4 shows how the ULA uses exactly this test.

Here is H taken apart:

$2D  =  0 0 101101
        │ │ └──┬─┘
        │ │    └── bits 0–5: character 45 → its shape is at $1E00 + 45 × 8 = $1F68
        │ └─────── bit 6: 0, a character to draw
        └───────── bit 7: 0, not inverted

So the word HELLO at the start of a line is stored like this:

 $2D   $2A   $31   $31   $34   ...   $76
  H     E     L     L     O    ...   NEWLINE

Now look at that $76 again with a Z80 programmer’s eyes. $76 is the opcode of HALT. That is no accident.

Part 4: The trick — the CPU executes the screen

When the ROM wants to draw the text lines, it does something that looks absurd: it jumps into the display file, as if the screen were code. Precisely, it jumps to D_FILE + $8000.

Why the + $8000? On a 1K or 16K ZX81 the RAM appears twice in the address map: once at $4000, and again as an echo above $8000, because the upper address lines are not decoded. Both addresses reach the same byte, but the second one has address line A15 high. The ULA watches A15 to tell “the CPU is running the screen” from “the CPU is running a program”.

What happens on every opcode fetch

Recall how a Z80 fetches an opcode. This is the M1 cycle, 4 T-states long:

  • T1–T2: the CPU puts PC on the address bus and reads the opcode byte from the data bus.
  • T3–T4: while it decodes the opcode, the CPU puts the refresh address on the address bus, I × 256 + R, so that dynamic RAM chips can refresh themselves. Then R is incremented.

To look the fetch up yourself, see Zilog’s Z80 CPU User Manual  (UM0080): the “Instruction Fetch” section and its Figure 5, “Instruction Op Code Fetch”, show the M1 cycle signal by signal. The same manual describes the R register (only its lower seven bits count) and the NOPs a halted CPU keeps executing, both of which this article relies on.

The ULA works its magic in both halves:

First half — steal the byte. If A15 is high and the fetched byte has bit 6 clear, the ULA:

  1. keeps a copy of the byte (it is a character code), and
  2. forces $00 onto the data bus instead.

The CPU never sees the character. It sees $00, which is NOP, executes it, and moves PC on to the next byte. Every character code, $00–$3F and $80–$BF, has bit 6 clear, so each one is stolen and becomes a NOP.

Second half — fetch the dots. During the refresh, the address bus carries I × 256 + R. The ULA keeps the top part (from the I register, which the ROM sets to $1E) but replaces the lower nine address bits with:

character code × 8  +  line within the character (0–7)

That is the address of one row of the character’s shape in the ROM’s character set at $1E00. The ROM answers with that row’s 8 bits, and the ULA loads them into a shift register. Over the next 4 T-states the shift register pushes the 8 bits out to the television, 2 per T-state: a 1 bit is a black dot, a 0 bit a white one, and bit 7 of the character code swaps them.

Put the two halves together and you get the key idea of the whole machine:

Each NOP the CPU “executes” in the display file draws one character’s 8 dots. 32 characters are 32 NOPs, 32 × 4 = 128 T-states, 256 dots: one scan line of text.

The CPU is the ZX81’s address counter. In a machine with a video chip, the chip has a counter of its own that steps through the screen memory, one address per character. The ZX81 has no such counter. Its job is done by the Z80’s program counter, the PC register:

  • PC holds the address of the next character. While the CPU runs the display file, PC always points at the next byte to fetch, and that byte is the next character on the line.
  • Every fetch shows it to the ULA. Each opcode fetch puts PC on the address bus, and that is how the character byte reaches the data bus and the ULA.
  • Every NOP moves it on by one. Executing a NOP adds 1 to PC, and takes 4 T-states, exactly the time the beam needs to draw one character.
  • A jump sets it. Loading PC with a line’s first address, with JP (HL), points the counter at the start of a line. Part 5 shows the ROM doing exactly this, to draw each line 8 times.

So the Z80’s ordinary instruction fetching is the display’s address counter: NOP steps it, and a jump reloads it.

Why bit 6, and why HALT survives

This is the bit 6 test from Part 3. The ULA only steals bytes with bit 6 clear, the characters. HALT is $76 = 0111 0110: bit 6 is set. So at the end of each line the ULA lets the byte through, and the CPU really executes a HALT. You will see in a moment that this is exactly what the ROM wants.

The rule has a price: real code cannot run above $8000 on a standard ZX81, because the ULA would turn most of its opcodes into NOPs.

A whole frame at a glance

You have now seen how the ULA turns one NOP into 8 dots, and how a line of characters becomes a run of NOPs ending in a HALT. Before zooming into how those lines are timed, here is the whole frame they live in.

A frame is more than the 192 lines of text. Around them, the television needs a VSYNC and some blank lines at the top and bottom: the border. The ROM builds the frame in this order:

  1. VSYNC and the keyboard. On the ZX81, reading port $FE (an IN with A0 low) reads the keyboard, and while the NMI generator is off, as it is at this point of the frame, it also starts VSYNC; any OUT then ends it and resets the line counter. The ROM reads the keyboard, waits in a short delay loop so VSYNC lasts long enough for the television to notice, then sends an OUT. (With the NMI generator on, an IN from port $FE only reads the keys: Part 7 comes back to this.)
  2. The top border: blank lines. Their number is the system variable MARGIN: 55 on a PAL machine, 31 on an NTSC one.
  3. The text: one blank line for the display file’s first $76, then 24 text lines of 8 scan lines each: 193 scan lines in all.
  4. The bottom border: another MARGIN blank lines.
  5. Back to step 1.

On a PAL machine this makes 311 scan lines, 311 × 207 = 64,377 T-states, about 19.8 ms: just over 50 frames a second.

The frame routine

These five steps are one ROM routine at $0229. Its first half is housekeeping: the FRAMES counter that PAUSE uses, reading the keyboard, and debouncing the keys. It is shortened here to the lines that matter for the picture:

; $0229: one frame of the picture
DisplayFrame:
    ld hl,($4034)     ; HL = FRAMES, the frame counter ...
    dec hl            ; ... counted down every frame (PAUSE uses it)
    ; ... $022D-$023D: FRAMES bookkeeping
    call $02BB        ; read the keyboard: its IN starts VSYNC
    ; ... $0241-$0276: debounce the key, and a DJNZ delay loop
    ;     that gives VSYNC its length
    out ($FF),a       ; any OUT ends VSYNC and resets the line counter
    ld hl,($400C)     ; HL = D_FILE ...
    set 7,h           ; ... + $8000: the display file's echo
    call BorderLines  ; the top border
    ld a,r            ; only for the timing
    ld bc,$1901       ; B = 25: the opening NEWLINE, then 24 text lines
                      ; C = 1: one scan line for the opening NEWLINE
    ld a,$F5          ; R for that first, empty line
    call DisplayLines ; the text
    dec hl            ; HL back on the display file's last NEWLINE
    call BorderLines  ; the bottom border
    jp DisplayFrame   ; the next frame

The two CALL BorderLines make the top and bottom borders, and CALL DisplayLines starts the text.

One endless loop, and your program as its guest

The frame routine, DisplayFrame at $0229, ends with a jump back to its own start. In SLOW mode, which is how a ZX81 normally runs, that makes it an endless loop. Once the ROM has started it, the CPU stays in it for good: every frame, forever, it draws the picture. Everything else the ZX81 does happens in the gaps of this loop: the BASIC editor, the BASIC interpreter running your program, and any machine code you call. That is the two orange bands of the picture above, the top and bottom borders.

So the display and your program take turns on one CPU, a little like two tasks in a tiny operating system. In SLOW mode, each CALL BorderLines is where the frame hands the CPU to your program; it gets the CPU back only when the border is over.

The next three parts follow the frame: Part 5 draws the blue band, the 193 lines of text; Part 6 makes the borders; and Part 7 puts together how the display and your program share the CPU.

Part 5: Drawing each line eight times

A character is 8 dots tall, so every text line needs 8 scan lines, and each of them shows a different row of the characters’ shapes. That means the CPU has to run the same display-file line 8 times, while something counts which row it is on.

The ULA’s two counters

The ULA keeps track of the beam with two counters. Their names are similar, but they count very different things.

The line timer measures time within a scan line. It counts T-states from 0 to 206, then wraps back to 0: one round is one 207 T-state line. The ULA makes HSYNC from it. At T-state 16 HSYNC starts, and at T-state 32 it ends and the beam starts a new line. The timer runs by itself, whatever the CPU is doing. It is how HSYNC keeps arriving every 64 µs, and (in SLOW mode) how the border NMIs of Part 6 arrive, since they come at the start of each HSYNC. One thing does reset it, though: the CPU accepting the display’s interrupt, as you will see in a moment. And there is one time when no HSYNC goes out at all: during VSYNC, which holds the output at the sync level until it ends. Normally that is only a few lines per frame, but in FAST mode it can last for as long as a program runs (see Part 7).

The line counter counts scan lines. It is 3 bits wide (0–7) and goes up by one every time HSYNC starts. It is the “line within the character” that the ULA adds to the character address. It is reset to 0 at the end of each VSYNC, and the ROM times the top border so that the counter has just wrapped back to 0 when the first text line starts.

So the hardware already knows which row of the shapes to fetch. The ROM’s job is to make sure the CPU runs each display-file line once per scan line, every 207 T-states, to the T-state.

Running a line: HALT and an interrupt on A6

Here is the clever part. When the CPU reaches the $76 at the end of a line, it executes HALT and stops. A halted Z80 does not quite stop, though: it keeps executing internal NOPs, one M1 cycle every 4 T-states, and each M1 still increments R and puts it on the address bus during refresh.

On the ZX81, the Z80’s INT pin is wired to address line A6. While the refresh address is on the bus, A6 carries bit 6 of R. So the moment R’s bit 6 goes to 0, an interrupt is requested.

But wait: A6 is just as often 0 at other moments too, for example while an opcode is fetched from an address with bit 6 clear. Why does that not cause an interrupt? Because the Z80 does not watch INT all the time. As Zilog’s manual  puts it, the CPU “samples the interrupt signal (INT) with the rising edge of the final clock at the end of any instruction”. While interrupts are on, the display runs only instructions that end with the refresh of their M1 cycle (EI, JP (HL), the stolen NOPs and the NOPs inside HALT). So at that one moment the address bus carries the refresh address, and A6 is bit 6 of R, not of PC. Everywhere else interrupts are simply switched off: the CPU ignores INT unless they have been enabled, and only the display code enables them, just before it runs a line.

R is a counter of M1 cycles, and the ROM can load it with LD R,A. So R is a countdown timer: load it with the right value, and the interrupt arrives after exactly the right number of opcode fetches. The ROM loads $DD into R before each line. Counting from there, the line’s 32 characters and its HALT take R up to $FF. The next M1, the first one inside the HALT, refreshes with R = $80: bit 6 is now 0, and INT fires.

Why $80 and not $00? Because the Z80 increments only the lower 7 bits of R, and bit 7 never changes when R counts: it keeps whatever LD R,A put there. So from $FF (bit 7 set, lower bits 111 1111) the lower 7 bits wrap round to 000 0000, while bit 7 stays 1, and R becomes $80. That step clears bit 6, the bit the interrupt is wired to. Why exactly $DD? That needs the interrupt routine, which comes next; the answer follows it, under “Why $DD?”.

The interrupt is the ROM’s routine at $0038 (the Z80 is in interrupt mode 1). Note what accepting the interrupt does first: it switches interrupts off. In the words of Zilog’s manual , “when the CPU accepts a maskable interrupt, both IFF1 and IFF2 are automatically reset, inhibiting further interrupts until the programmer issues a new EI instruction”. So the routine runs undisturbed and needs no DI, and the next interrupt can come only after the EI in RunLine. Even then, the manual adds, not before the instruction that follows the EI has run, which here is the JP (HL) into the line. Disassembled, with names of our own:

; $0038: one interrupt per scan line of text
; B = text lines left, C = scan lines left of this text line
; HL = start of this line in the display file, A = $DD
IntDisplay:
    dec c            ; one more scan line of this text line done
    jp nz,SameLine   ; scan lines left: run the same line again
    pop hl           ; HL = the address after the HALT: the next line
    dec b            ; one more text line done
    ret z            ; no lines left: the text area is finished
    set 3,c          ; C = 8 scan lines for the new text line
RunLine:
    ld r,a           ; restart the countdown: R = $DD
    ei               ; let the next INT in
    jp (hl)          ; "execute" the line: 32 NOPs, then HALT
SameLine:
    pop de           ; drop the return address; HL still points
                     ; at this line's first character
    ret z            ; never taken: only here to keep the timing equal
    jr RunLine

The routine takes one of two paths, depending on whether the current text line needs another scan line.

Every interrupt starts here.

IntDisplay:
    dec c            ; one more scan line of this text line done
    jp nz,SameLine   ; scan lines left: run the same line again

C counts the scan lines still to draw for the current text line: 8 at the start of each one. While some are left, the routine jumps to SameLine.

Path 1: the same line again.

SameLine:
    pop de           ; drop the return address; HL still points
                     ; at this line's first character
    ret z            ; never taken: only here to keep the timing equal
    jr RunLine

Accepting the interrupt pushed the address just after the HALT. This path does not need it, because HL still points at the first character of the line being repeated, so POP DE throws it away. The RET Z is never taken (see “Why the interrupt routine saves no registers” below); it is there only to make this path as long as the other one. Then the routine runs the same line again.

Path 2: the next line.

    pop hl           ; HL = the address after the HALT: the next line
    dec b            ; one more text line done
    ret z            ; no lines left: the text area is finished
    set 3,c          ; C = 8 scan lines for the new text line

When C reaches 0, the current text line has had its 8 scan lines. The address the interrupt pushed, just after this line’s HALT, is exactly the first character of the next line, so POP HL takes it as the new line’s start. B counts the text lines still to draw, and when it reaches 0 the text is finished and RET Z leaves the loop. Otherwise SET 3,C turns C’s 0 into 8 for the new line.

Both paths end here.

RunLine:
    ld r,a           ; restart the countdown: R = $DD
    ei               ; let the next INT in
    jp (hl)          ; "execute" the line: 32 NOPs, then HALT

LD R,A restarts the countdown that will end the next scan line (why it is $DD is explained below), EI lets that interrupt in, and JP (HL) runs the line.

Whichever way the routine goes, it takes exactly the same time. Add up one whole scan line, from one interrupt to the next:

StepT-states
Accept the interrupt (IM 1: push PC, jump to $0038)13
DEC C + JP NZ4 + 10 = 14
Either path 1, the same line again: POP DE + RET Z (not taken) + JR10 + 5 + 12 = 27
or path 2, the next line: POP HL + DEC B + RET Z (not taken) + SET 3,C10 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 27
LD R,A + EI + JP (HL)9 + 4 + 4 = 17
32 characters, each a NOP128
HALT4
One more NOP inside the HALT: R’s bit 6 is 0, INT fires4
One scan line207

207 T-states: exactly one PAL line. Only one of the two paths runs on any interrupt, so only one of them is counted; both take 27 T-states, which is the point.

Short lines and empty lines. The table assumes a full line of 32 characters. On a 1K ZX81 that would waste memory, so the ROM collapses the display file (Part 3): a line holds its characters only up to the last one that is not a space, and an empty line is nothing but its NEWLINE, a bare HALT. Such a line still lasts exactly 207 T-states, because what ends it is not the HALT but the R countdown. A halted CPU keeps making one M1 cycle every 4 T-states, just as the missing NOPs would have. A line of 5 characters reaches its HALT 27 M1 cycles sooner and spends them inside the HALT instead; a bare NEWLINE spends all 32 there. Either way the interrupt comes at the same moment (“Why $DD?” below counts the cycles). And the ULA draws nothing for the missing characters, because it only draws the bytes it steals, so the rest of the line simply shows paper.

Klive shows it on its 1K model. After PRINT "HELLO" the whole display file is 33 bytes: 25 NEWLINEs, 5 characters on the first line and 3 on the last (the “0/0” report), with every line in between a bare NEWLINE. Every text line still lasts exactly 207 T-states.

This is the sum for every line that is drawn, and on those lines neither RET Z is taken: a RET Z that does not return takes 5 T-states. The very last interrupt of the text area is the exception. There B reaches 0, the RET Z after DEC B is taken (11 T-states), and SET 3,C and RunLine never run. That interrupt starts no new line: it ends the text and returns to the frame routine.

This different path does not disturb the picture. It changes only what the CPU does next, not the sync: the ULA’s line timer keeps making HSYNC every 207 T-states by itself, and this last interrupt was accepted at the usual moment of its line anyway. And nothing is drawn after it: the ULA only draws the bytes it steals from the display file, so the bottom border shows plain paper whatever the CPU is doing. The next line with characters on it is the first text line of the next frame, and that one is lined up afresh, in SLOW mode by the HALT in NmiLast waiting for an NMI (Part 6).

The interrupt does one more thing: when the CPU acknowledges it, the ULA resets its line timer (the counter that makes HSYNC, from “The ULA’s two counters” above). HSYNC therefore starts 16 T-states later, while the CPU is still inside the interrupt routine. So the routine’s own running time becomes the left border, and each line of text starts at the same horizontal position, line after line.

Why $DD?

Now that the whole loop is on the page, back to the value RunLine loads into R:

RunLine:
    ld r,a           ; restart the countdown: R = $DD
    ei               ; let the next INT in
    jp (hl)          ; "execute" the line: 32 NOPs, then HALT

Where does A get $DD? Once, from the routine that starts the text, in the next subsection. Nothing in the loop changes A after that: the interrupt routine never touches it, and neither do the NOPs and the HALT. So every LD R,A in RunLine, on every line, loads $DD.

The trick is to read that value as minus the number of M1 cycles to wait.

As you saw above, bit 7 of R never changes when R counts. So if bit 7 is set, R climbs to $FF and then wraps round to $80, the first value on its way with bit 6 clear. Load R with $100 − n, and exactly n M1 cycles refresh with bit 6 still set; the one after them fires INT. (The two M1 cycles of LD R,A itself do not count: they happen before R is written.)

$DD is $100 − 35, and a text line has exactly 35 M1 cycles before the one that should end it:

After LD R,A in RunLineM1 cycles
EI1
JP (HL)1
32 characters, each a NOP32
The HALT at the end of the line1
Total35

The 36th M1, the first NOP inside the HALT, fires INT.

The count does not care what is in the line, because a halted CPU also makes one M1 every 4 T-states: a short or empty line just spends more of its 35 cycles inside the HALT, as shown above. Either way the 36th M1 comes at the same moment, so every line lasts 207 T-states, full, short or empty.

Starting the text: DisplayLines

The line loop needs a first push: someone has to set its registers and jump to the first line. The frame routine does it, with these lines from its listing in Part 4:

    ld a,r            ; only for the timing
    ld bc,$1901       ; B = 25: the opening NEWLINE, then 24 text lines
                      ; C = 1: one scan line for the opening NEWLINE
    ld a,$F5          ; R for that first, empty line
    call DisplayLines ; the text

They are the loop’s starting values: B counts 25 lines, the display file’s opening NEWLINE and then the 24 text lines; C gives the first of them a single scan line; and A holds the R countdown for that first line. HL was set to D_FILE + $8000, the opening NEWLINE, before the top border. Then DisplayLines gets the loop going:

; $02B5: start running the display file at HL (the borders use it too)
DisplayLines:
    ld r,a           ; R: when the first INT comes
    ld a,$DD         ; R for every line after it
    ei
    jp (hl)

It loads the first countdown into R, leaves $DD in A for every line after the first, enables the interrupt and jumps into the display file. The opening NEWLINE is a HALT, so the first “line” draws nothing; its interrupt then runs path 2 of the interrupt routine, which sets C to 8 for the first real text line. From there, the interrupt routine runs everything.

Why $F5 for the first line? By the rule of “Why $DD?”, $F5 is $100 − 11: after LD R,A, eleven M1 cycles pass (LD A,$DD, EI, JP (HL), the opening HALT and seven NOPs inside it), and the eighth NOP fires INT. Why eleven? In SLOW mode the text starts at a precise moment of the line, thanks to a HALT and the ULA’s WAIT at the end of the top border (Part 6 shows how). So the ROM can choose the count that makes this first, empty line exactly as long as a normal one. You can see this in Klive: when the ULA’s line timer is read as each interrupt is accepted, the text’s first interrupt comes at the same point of the line (T-state 202 of 207) as every interrupt after it. The hand-over from the border to the text does not leave a single short or long line. After this first line, $DD does the rest.

Why the interrupt routine saves no registers

A textbook interrupt handler starts with PUSHes, ends with POPs and RETI, and assumes nothing about the registers it finds, because it can arrive in the middle of any program. The ZX81’s $0038 routine does none of this. It changes B, C, HL and DE freely, it relies on A holding $DD, and it never returns to where it was called from. This is safe for four reasons.

1. It only ever interrupts its own code. The Z80 accepts a maskable interrupt only after EI, and turns interrupts off again whenever it accepts one. The only EI in this loop is in RunLine, just before JP (HL) jumps into the display file. So the one thing this interrupt can ever interrupt is the HALT at the end of a display-file line.

The routine has two RET Zs, but only one of them is a way out. The one in SameLine is never taken:

SameLine:
    pop de           ; drop the return address; HL still points
                     ; at this line's first character
    ret z            ; never taken: only here to keep the timing equal
    jr RunLine

The routine gets there only when DEC C has just produced a non-zero result, so Z is always clear, and the instruction is there only for its 5 T-states. The real exit is the RET Z straight after DEC B:

    pop hl           ; HL = the address after the HALT: the next line
    dec b            ; one more text line done
    ret z            ; no lines left: the text area is finished

It is taken when B reaches 0, on the interrupt after the last scan line of the last text line. It leaves without passing the EI in RunLine, so interrupts stay off for the rest of the frame. A program in RAM can therefore never trigger the A6 interrupt by accident.

2. The registers belong to the display loop. The “program” being interrupted is 32 NOPs and a HALT, which change no registers at all (except R and PC). B, C, HL and A are not someone else’s registers that the routine must leave alone. They are the loop variables of the ROM’s own display code, set up before the first line (LD BC,$1901, LD A,$F5, HL = D_FILE + $8000). Think of the whole thing as one loop whose “jump back to the top” happens to be a hardware interrupt: each interrupt is simply the loop’s next pass.

3. Even the return address is data. When the Z80 accepts the interrupt it pushes PC, which points just after the HALT: that is, at the first byte of the next line. The routine uses that directly. It either keeps it as the next line’s address (POP HL) or throws it away to draw the same line again (POP DE). It never returns there. On the way to the exit, POP HL has already taken that address off the stack, so the stack now holds the return address of the CALL that started the text. The RET Z after DEC B returns from that call, back into the frame routine.

4. There is no time. A line has 207 T-states. The characters take 128 and the HALT and its NOP another 8, which leaves 71 T-states for accepting the interrupt, the routine, and restarting the line. Those 71 T-states are the left border. Pushing and popping just AF, BC, DE and HL would cost 4 × 11 + 4 × 10 = 84 T-states: more than the whole budget.

Your program’s own registers are a different story: they are saved while the display runs, and Part 7 shows where.

Part 6: The borders

Part 4 ended with the map of a frame, and Part 5 drew the text in its middle. This part makes the rest: the blank lines of the top and bottom borders, which in SLOW mode are also when your program runs.

Two kinds of border

How a border is made depends on the ZX81’s mode, which you choose with the BASIC commands SLOW and FAST, and which bit 7 of the system variable CDFLAG records:

  • In SLOW mode, the normal one, your program runs during the borders, while the hardware counts the blank lines with NMIs.
  • In FAST mode there are no NMIs. The ROM draws frames only while it waits for a key, and it makes their borders with the same line loop that draws the text.

BorderLines handles both. Part 7 compares the two modes in full.

The border: NMIs count the lines while your program runs

During the text, the CPU is completely busy. But a border line shows nothing, so there is no point in the CPU walking through anything. The ZX81 uses those lines to run your program, and lets the hardware count them.

The ULA has an NMI generator: when it is switched on (an OUT to port $FE), the ULA raises the Z80’s non-maskable interrupt at the start of every HSYNC; an OUT to port $FD switches it off. A border is a hand-over in three steps: the frame routine gives the CPU to your program, NMIs count the blank lines while the program runs, and the last NMI takes the CPU back.

Entering the border: the frame parks its place in IX

The frame routine draws each border with a CALL BorderLines (see its listing in Part 4), the routine at $0292. Here is all of it, with the FAST-mode border that follows it in the ROM:

; $0292: a border of MARGIN blank lines (SLOW mode)
BorderLines:
    pop ix           ; IX = where the frame goes on after the border
    ld c,(iy+$28)    ; C = MARGIN (IY points at the system variables)
    bit 7,(iy+$3B)   ; CDFLAG bit 7: SLOW mode running?
    jr z,FastBorder  ; no: FAST mode makes its border differently
    ld a,c
    neg
    inc a            ; A = 1 - MARGIN
    ex af,af'        ; ... into A', the line counter
    out ($FE),a      ; NMI generator on
    pop hl           ; your program's registers back
    pop de
    pop bc
    pop af
    ret              ; ... and back into your program
 
; $02A9: the border in FAST mode
FastBorder:
    ld a,$FC         ; R for the first blank line
    ld b,1           ; one "text line" ...
    call DisplayLines ; ... of C = MARGIN scan lines
    dec hl           ; HL back on the NEWLINE
    ex (sp),hl       ; these two cancel out:
    ex (sp),hl       ; they are only here for their timing
    jp (ix)          ; carry on with the frame

The rest of this subsection takes the listing a few lines at a time, repeating each piece next to its explanation.

Step 1: the bookmark.

BorderLines:
    pop ix           ; IX = where the frame goes on after the border

A subroutine normally ends with RET to its caller. This one takes its own return address off the stack first and keeps it in IX. That address is the frame routine’s bookmark: the instruction after the CALL, where the frame continues once the border is over. Whichever kind of border follows, it ends with JP (IX) back to that bookmark.

Step 2: which kind of border?

    ld c,(iy+$28)    ; C = MARGIN (IY points at the system variables)
    bit 7,(iy+$3B)   ; CDFLAG bit 7: SLOW mode running?
    jr z,FastBorder  ; no: FAST mode makes its border differently

IY always holds $4000, the start of the system variables, so (IY+$28) is MARGIN at $4028 and (IY+$3B) is CDFLAG at $403B. C now holds the number of blank lines to make, 55 on a PAL machine, and both kinds of border use it. Bit 7 of CDFLAG says whether SLOW mode is running. If it is not, the routine goes on at FastBorder (step 5).

Step 3: SLOW mode, arm the line counter.

    ld a,c
    neg
    inc a            ; A = 1 - MARGIN
    ex af,af'        ; ... into A', the line counter
    out ($FE),a      ; NMI generator on

NEG and INC A turn MARGIN into 1 − MARGIN: for 55, that is −54. The line count goes into A′, the alternate accumulator, which BASIC does not use. Every border NMI adds one to it, so it counts up towards 0, and reaching 0 ends the border. The OUT to port $FE switches the NMI generator on: from the next HSYNC, the NMIs start counting.

Step 4: SLOW mode, return into your program.

    pop hl           ; your program's registers back
    pop de
    pop bc
    pop af
    ret              ; ... and back into your program

With the bookmark taken off the stack in step 1, the stack underneath holds your program’s registers and the address your program was interrupted at. So these POPs and this RET return into your program, not to the frame routine. This is the switch from the display task to the program task; Part 7 puts all the switches side by side, under Switching tasks.

One side effect: the frame routine had set HL to the display file before the CALL, and POP HL replaces it with your program’s HL. That is why NmiLast has to load D_FILE + $8000 into HL again before the text.

Step 5: FAST mode, set up the parameters.

FastBorder:
    ld a,$FC         ; R for the first blank line
    ld b,1           ; one "text line" ...
    call DisplayLines ; ... of C = MARGIN scan lines

In FAST mode there are no NMIs, so BorderLines keeps the CPU and comes here. It makes the blank lines with the text machinery from Part 5: DisplayLines and the interrupt routine. These first lines do no work of their own; they set up the parameters that machinery works with:

  • LD A,$FC passes the starting value for R. DisplayLines begins with LD R,A, so this $FC becomes the R countdown for the first blank line. Step 6 shows why it is $FC.
  • LD B,1 says there is one “text line” to run.
  • C already holds MARGIN, from step 2: the number of scan lines to give that one line.
  • HL is left as the frame routine set it: where in the display file to run.

FastBorder does not touch HL before the CALL, so HL points at a NEWLINE in the display file:

  • for the top border, the opening NEWLINE, because the frame routine set HL to D_FILE + $8000 just before CALL BorderLines;
  • for the bottom border, the display file’s last NEWLINE, because the frame routine stepped HL back onto it with DEC HL after the text.

This is exactly how the frame routine starts the text (Part 5), only with other values.

Step 6: the line loop runs the blank lines.

DisplayLines (Part 5) loads the countdown into R, leaves $DD in A for the interrupt routine, enables interrupts and jumps to HL. For a border, HL points at a NEWLINE, so JP (HL) runs straight into a HALT, and the “line” draws nothing. With B = 1 and C = MARGIN, the interrupt routine runs that empty line MARGIN times, one scan line each.

The two values for R follow the rule from Part 5: load R with $100 − n to let n M1 cycles pass before the one that fires INT.

  • $FC = $100 − 4 is for the first blank line only. After LD R,A, four M1 cycles pass before the HALT’s inside: LD A,$DD, EI, JP (HL) and the HALT itself. (Unlike the interrupt routine’s RunLine, DisplayLines has that extra LD A,$DD between LD R,A and EI.) The first NOP inside the HALT then fires INT, just as on every other line. The count is short because the line is empty: there are no characters to wait for.
  • $DD = $100 − 35 is for every line after that. DisplayLines leaves it in A, and the interrupt routine loads it into R before each line. It is the same value the text uses, and as Part 5 showed, it makes an empty line exactly as long as a full one: 207 T-states.

The first blank line is not a full line. In FAST mode nothing has lined the CPU up with the ULA’s line timer before this point, so that first interrupt arrives at a different point of the line each time. That does not matter: accepting it resets the ULA’s line timer, and from then on the CPU and the lines run in step. The text’s first line is the opposite case: there the start is precise, and the ROM uses $F5 instead to make that line exactly as long as all the others (Part 5).

Step 7: FAST mode, back to the frame.

    dec hl           ; HL back on the NEWLINE
    ex (sp),hl       ; these two cancel out:
    ex (sp),hl       ; they are only here for their timing
    jp (ix)          ; carry on with the frame

On the border’s last scan line, the interrupt routine’s POP HL loads the address just past the NEWLINE, and its RET Z returns here, to the instruction after CALL DisplayLines. DEC HL puts HL back on the NEWLINE. After the top border, that is exactly D_FILE + $8000 again: the address the frame routine’s own CALL DisplayLines needs to start the text. The two EX (SP),HL swap HL with the top of the stack and back again, changing nothing but spending 38 T-states. Then JP (IX) returns to the bookmark from step 1, just as a SLOW-mode border does at its end.

Counting the lines

Now your program runs, and at every HSYNC an NMI interrupts it. Each one lands at $0066:

; $0066: one NMI per border line
Nmi:
    ex af,af'        ; A' is the border line counter
    inc a            ; one more blank line
    jp m,NmiReturn   ; still negative: more lines to go
    jr z,NmiLast     ; zero: this was the last border line
NmiReturn:
    ex af,af'
    ret              ; back to the program
NmiLast:
    ex af,af'
    push af          ; save the program's registers
    push bc
    push de
    push hl
    ld hl,($400C)    ; HL = D_FILE
    set 7,h          ; ... + $8000: the display file's echo
    halt             ; wait for the next NMI
    out ($FD),a      ; NMI generator off
    jp (ix)          ; carry on with the frame

For most NMIs only the first five instructions run:

Nmi:
    ex af,af'        ; A' is the border line counter
    inc a            ; one more blank line
    jp m,NmiReturn   ; still negative: more lines to go
    jr z,NmiLast     ; zero: this was the last border line
NmiReturn:
    ex af,af'
    ret              ; back to the program

They save nothing because they need nothing: EX AF,AF' swaps your program’s A and flags out of the way and the counter in, and the second EX AF,AF' swaps them back. Your program’s registers are never touched.

Leaving the border: NmiLast

When the count reaches 0, the border is over and the NMI routine falls into NmiLast, which turns the CPU back over to the frame. This is the switch from the program task back to the display task; Part 7 puts all the switches side by side, under Switching tasks. Here is that part of the routine again:

NmiLast:
    ex af,af'
    push af          ; save the program's registers
    push bc
    push de
    push hl
    ld hl,($400C)    ; HL = D_FILE
    set 7,h          ; ... + $8000: the display file's echo
    halt             ; wait for the next NMI
    out ($FD),a      ; NMI generator off
    jp (ix)          ; carry on with the frame

Step by step:

  1. The NMI pushed your program’s PC when it was accepted. That is where your program will carry on next time.
  2. PUSH AF … PUSH HL save your program’s registers on top of it. The stack now holds exactly what BorderLines pops and returns through when the next border begins.
  3. LD HL,(D_FILE) and SET 7,H set HL to the display file’s echo above $8000. The frame routine had already set HL before calling BorderLines, but BorderLines gave HL back to your program, so NmiLast has to set it again for the text that follows.
  4. HALT waits for one more NMI, so that the text starts at a precise moment. The next subsection explains why. That NMI comes in at $0066 again: the count goes from 0 to 1, which is neither negative nor zero, so it leaves through NmiReturn and its RET lands on the instruction after the HALT.
  5. OUT ($FD),A switches the NMI generator off: the text must not be interrupted.
  6. JP (IX) jumps to the frame routine’s bookmark, just after its CALL BorderLines.

Why JP (IX) and not RET? Because the top of the stack is now your program’s saved state, not a return address into the frame routine. The bookmark could not wait on the stack, because your program was using the stack all through the border. So the frame routine keeps it in a register that your program is not supposed to touch.

When the frame reaches the next border, BorderLines finds the stack like this, top first:

SP →  return address of CALL BorderLines    → POP IX: the new bookmark
      HL ┐                                  → POP HL
      DE │ your program's registers,        → POP DE
      BC │ pushed by NmiLast                → POP BC
      AF ┘                                  → POP AF
      your program's PC, pushed by the NMI  → RET: back into your program

The very first time, the ROM routine that starts SLOW mode pushes the same four registers before it enters the frame. The first border finds the stack in the same shape, and its RET returns to whoever started SLOW mode.

This is why machine code running in SLOW mode must leave IX alone: it holds the bookmark that NmiLast jumps through. If your code changes IX, the next JP (IX) jumps into whatever IX now points at. IY must be left alone too: BorderLines reads MARGIN and CDFLAG through it.

Your program gets the time between NMIs. So in SLOW mode a program runs only during the borders: a little over a third of the frame, minus the time the NMIs themselves take. That is the price of a steady picture, and why programs run about 3.75 times slower in SLOW mode than in FAST mode.

The HALT that keeps the picture still

Look at NmiLast again. Before handing over to the text, it executes a HALT. Why wait for one more NMI instead of starting the text right away?

Because an NMI interrupts whatever instruction your program happens to be running, and the Z80 only responds when that instruction is finished. A NOP finishes within 4 T-states; an EX (SP),HL takes 19. If the text started straight from such an NMI, it would start a few T-states early or late in a different place each frame, and the whole picture would shimmer sideways by a few dots.

The HALT removes most of the uncertainty: a halted CPU only runs internal NOPs, so it starts responding to the next NMI within 4 T-states. The ULA removes the rest with the Z80’s WAIT pin. While the NMI line is active and the CPU is not halted, the ULA holds WAIT, which freezes the current bus cycle. The moment the CPU starts its NMI response it is no longer halted, so it is frozen until HSYNC ends. “Within 4 T-states” becomes “exactly at the end of HSYNC”, the CPU leaves the HALT at the same T-state of the line every frame, and the text that follows lines up perfectly.

Part 7: Sharing the CPU

Everything so far has been about the display. But a ZX81 also has to run your program, on the same Z80, and Parts 5 and 6 have shown that the display needs that Z80 for most of every frame. This part puts the pieces together: how the CPU passes between your program and the display. The two modes do it in completely different ways:

SLOW modeFAST mode
Who is in chargeThe display: an endless loop that never stopsThe ROM’s BASIC system and your program
How the display runsAs a task of its own, taking turns with your programAs an ordinary subroutine, called only while the ROM waits for a key or a PAUSE
How the CPU changes handsA task switch, four times a frame: an NMI takes the CPU from your program, a RET gives it backA CALL and a RET
What is savedYour program’s PC, AF, BC, DE and HL, on its own stackOnly the CALL’s return address
Your program’s share of the CPUAbout a quarter on PAL (measured: 26.7%), a sixth on NTSC (17.3%)All of it, but no picture while it runs
What you seeA steady picture, but programs run nearly 4 times slower (nearly 6 on NTSC)The screen goes blank while a program runs, and flashes each time you press a key

A ZX81 starts up in SLOW mode. The system variable CDFLAG remembers the choice: bit 6 means “SLOW mode wanted”, bit 7 “SLOW mode running”. Before it starts SLOW mode, the ROM checks that the hardware actually produces display NMIs (“Starting and stopping the loop” below shows how).

The ZX80, the ZX81’s predecessor, has no NMI generator at all. It can only ever work like a ZX81 in FAST mode: the picture disappears whenever the machine is computing.

SLOW mode: two tasks on one CPU

In SLOW mode the frame routine is the endless loop of Part 4, and everything else happens in its gaps. Think of it as two tasks sharing one CPU, as in a tiny operating system with a fixed timetable:

The display taskThe program task
What it isThe ROM’s display code: DisplayFrame and the routines it callsEverything else: the ROM’s BASIC system, your BASIC program, your machine code
When it has the CPUVSYNC and the keyboard read, and the 193 lines of textThe two borders, about 110 lines of every frame
Where its place is kept while the other task runsIn IXOn the stack: its PC, and AF, BC, DE and HL
How it gives the CPU awayVoluntarily: it returns into the program task at the start of each borderIt does not. The hardware takes the CPU from it with an NMI at the end of each border

One frame, as the CPU sees it

Here is one PAL frame in order, with the moments when the CPU changes hands:

Part of the frameWho has the CPU
VSYNC and the keyboard read (a few lines)the display
switch: BorderLines returns into your program
Top border, 55 linesyour program, while the NMIs count the lines
switch: the last NMI, NmiLast jumps back into the display
Text, 193 linesthe display
switch: BorderLines returns into your program
Bottom border, 55 linesyour program, while the NMIs count the lines
switch: the last NMI, NmiLast jumps back into the display
… and the next frame begins with VSYNCthe display

Switching tasks

A switch means saving one task’s state and restoring the other’s, so that each carries on exactly where it stopped, as if nothing had happened. The ZX81 does it four times a frame, twice in each direction, with a handful of instructions. Part 6 showed them in their routines; here they are side by side.

From the display to the program, at the start of each border. BorderLines has already stored the display task’s place in IX and set the hardware counting the border lines. Its last lines restore your program:

    pop hl           ; your program's registers back
    pop de
    pop bc
    pop af
    ret              ; ... and back into your program

The POPs restore your program’s registers, and the RET takes your program’s saved PC off the stack: the program carries on exactly where it was stopped, one border earlier.

From the program back to the display, at the end of each border. The NMI for the last border line arrives in the middle of whatever your program is doing. Accepting it pushes the program’s PC, and the NMI routine does the rest:

NmiLast:
    ex af,af'
    push af          ; save the program's registers
    push bc
    push de
    push hl
    ld hl,($400C)    ; HL = D_FILE
    set 7,h          ; ... + $8000: the display file's echo
    halt             ; wait for the next NMI
    out ($FD),a      ; NMI generator off
    jp (ix)          ; carry on with the frame

The PUSHes save your program’s registers on top of its PC, and JP (IX) resumes the display task where it left off. (The HALT in between only lines the text up with HSYNC, as Part 6 explains.)

The program task is pre-empted: it never offers the CPU and cannot refuse it, just like a task stopped by a timer interrupt in a modern operating system. The display task, on the other hand, always hands the CPU over itself, at a moment of its own choosing.

One stack for both

The two tasks do not have separate stacks. The display task simply runs on top of the program’s stack:

        ... whatever your program had on its stack ...
        your program's PC          ← pushed when the NMI was accepted
        AF, BC, DE, HL             ← your program's registers, saved by the NMI routine
SP →    the display task's own return addresses and interrupts, while it runs

Everything the display task pushes it also pops before it hands the CPU back. So when the program runs again, its stack is exactly as it left it. This is why a program needs some free stack below SP at all times: the display task borrows that space twice a frame.

What is not saved

Only PC, AF, BC, DE and HL are saved, because saving costs time, and time is what the program task is short of. Everything else the two tasks must simply not fight over: IX, AF′, IY, I and the interrupt setting all belong to the display. Rules for your programs, at the end of this part, lists them with their reasons.

How much slower?

In FAST mode a running program has the whole CPU. In SLOW mode it only has the borders, and even there each border line costs an NMI (Part 6 shows its code). For a PAL machine:

T-states per frame
The whole frame: 311 lines × 20764,377
The top and bottom borders: 2 × 55 lines × 20722,770
One NMI per border line: 110 × (11 to accept it + 32 to count the line)− 4,730
Left for your program, at most18,040

That is 28% of the frame, so on paper SLOW mode is about 64,377 / 18,040 ≈ 3.6 times slower. The real figure is a little worse. The ULA’s WAIT (explained under “The HALT that keeps the picture still” in Part 6) can freeze your program for part of each HSYNC, and handing the CPU back and forth at the start and end of every border takes time too.

Klive can measure it. A machine-code loop (INC HL, then JP back to it) gets 26.7% of the T-states in SLOW mode and all of them in FAST mode. FAST mode runs it 3.75 times faster. BASIC is itself machine code in the ROM, so it slows down by about the same factor.

An NTSC machine fares worse. It draws the same 193 text lines in a shorter frame, 263 lines with 31-line borders, so the borders, your program’s time, shrink. On paper a program gets at most 18.7% of the frame, about 5.4 times slower than in FAST mode. Measured on Klive’s NTSC model, the same loop gets 17.3%: FAST mode runs it 5.8 times faster.

Starting and stopping the loop

The very first switch has to be faked, because there is no display task yet to switch from. At the end of start-up, the ROM calls the routine that starts SLOW mode:

; $0207: start SLOW mode, if it is wanted and the NMIs work
SlowFast:
    ld hl,$403B      ; HL = CDFLAG
    ld a,(hl)
    rla
    xor (hl)
    rla              ; carry = bit 6 XOR bit 7 of CDFLAG
    ret nc           ; "wanted" and "running" agree: nothing to do
    ld a,$7F
    ex af,af'        ; A' = $7F: each NMI adds one to it
    ld b,$11
    out ($FE),a      ; NMI generator on ...
SfWait:
    djnz SfWait      ; ... for a short wait ...
    out ($FD),a      ; ... and off again
    ex af,af'
    rla              ; carry = bit 7: did $7F become $80?
    jr nc,StayFast   ; no NMI came: stay in FAST mode
    set 7,(hl)       ; CDFLAG bit 7: SLOW mode running
    push af          ; the program task's registers ...
    push bc
    push de
    push hl
    jr $0229         ; ... and into DisplayFrame, the endless loop
StayFast:
    res 6,(hl)       ; SLOW mode no longer wanted
    ret

Step 1: is there anything to do?

    ld hl,$403B      ; HL = CDFLAG
    ld a,(hl)
    rla
    xor (hl)
    rla              ; carry = bit 6 XOR bit 7 of CDFLAG
    ret nc           ; "wanted" and "running" agree: nothing to do

RLA, XOR (HL) and RLA compare bit 6 of CDFLAG (“SLOW mode wanted”) with bit 7 (“SLOW mode running”). If they agree, SLOW mode is either running already or not wanted at all, and RET NC returns at once.

Step 2: do the NMIs work?

    ld a,$7F
    ex af,af'        ; A' = $7F: each NMI adds one to it
    ld b,$11
    out ($FE),a      ; NMI generator on ...
SfWait:
    djnz SfWait      ; ... for a short wait ...
    out ($FD),a      ; ... and off again
    ex af,af'
    rla              ; carry = bit 7: did $7F become $80?
    jr nc,StayFast   ; no NMI came: stay in FAST mode

Before it starts SLOW mode, the routine checks that the hardware really makes display NMIs. It puts $7F in A′ and switches the NMI generator on for 17 rounds of DJNZ: 216 T-states, a little more than one 207 T-state line, so at least one HSYNC, and with it one NMI, must come. Each NMI runs the NMI routine of Part 6, which adds one to A′ and, since the count is negative, returns at once. Then the generator is switched off again. If at least one NMI came, $7F has become $80, and the second RLA moves that bit 7 into carry.

Step 3: the fake switch.

    set 7,(hl)       ; CDFLAG bit 7: SLOW mode running
    push af          ; the program task's registers ...
    push bc
    push de
    push hl
    jr $0229         ; ... and into DisplayFrame, the endless loop

If NMIs do come, the routine marks SLOW mode as running, pushes AF, BC, DE and HL on top of its own return address, and jumps into DisplayFrame. To the display task that looks exactly like a program stopped by an NMI. So when the first top border begins and BorderLines “returns” to the program, it lands just after the CALL of this routine, and the start-up code carries on into the BASIC main loop, now as the program task. On Klive this first jump to DisplayFrame happens about 585 ms after power-on.

Step 4: no NMIs, stay in FAST mode.

StayFast:
    res 6,(hl)       ; SLOW mode no longer wanted
    ret

A ZX80 fitted with the ZX81 ROM has no NMI generator, so no NMI comes, and the routine clears the “SLOW mode wanted” bit: the machine gives SLOW mode up for good and works in FAST mode only.

Stopping. When the ROM needs the CPU to itself (to SAVE, LOAD or print, where every T-state must be its own), the program task stops the loop with this routine:

; $02E7: stop SLOW mode for now
SetFast:
    bit 7,(iy+$3B)   ; CDFLAG bit 7: SLOW mode running?
    ret z            ; no: nothing to stop
    halt             ; wait for the next NMI
    out ($FD),a      ; NMI generator off
    res 7,(iy+$3B)   ; SLOW mode no longer running
    ret

It runs during a border, as all program-task code does. HALT waits for the next border NMI, and then the NMI generator is switched off, and bit 7 of CDFLAG says SLOW mode is no longer running. The display task never gets its last NMI, so it is never resumed: it is simply abandoned, along with its place in IX. When the work is done, the ROM calls $0207 again, and a fresh loop starts exactly as it did at start-up.

FAST mode: the display as a subroutine

In FAST mode there is no endless loop and no task switching. The ROM’s BASIC system has the CPU all the time, and it runs the display only when it has nothing better to do: while it waits for a key, or for a PAUSE to run out.

Waiting for a key

The ROM waits for every key press here, in SLOW and in FAST mode alike:

; $04C1: wait for a key (its handling follows)
WaitKey:
    ld hl,$0000
    ld ($4018),hl    ; X_PTR = 0: no syntax error marker
    ld hl,$403B      ; HL = CDFLAG
    bit 7,(hl)       ; SLOW mode running?
    call z,$0229     ; no, FAST mode: show the picture until a key comes
KwLoop:
    bit 0,(hl)       ; CDFLAG bit 0: a new, steady key reading?
    jr z,KwLoop      ; not yet: wait
    ld bc,($4025)    ; BC = LAST_K, the reading

The choice.

    bit 7,(hl)       ; SLOW mode running?
    call z,$0229     ; no, FAST mode: show the picture until a key comes

In SLOW mode bit 7 of CDFLAG is set, and the CALL Z is skipped: the display is already running, as its own task. In FAST mode the CALL Z calls DisplayFrame as an ordinary subroutine, and that call does not come back until a key has been read.

The wait.

KwLoop:
    bit 0,(hl)       ; CDFLAG bit 0: a new, steady key reading?
    jr z,KwLoop      ; not yet: wait

In SLOW mode this little loop is where the key wait really waits. But nothing in the loop can ever change bit 0 of CDFLAG. Something else must, and it does so between two of the loop’s instructions. That is possible because the loop is program-task code: twice a frame, at the end of each border, an NMI takes the CPU away from it (see “Switching tasks” above). One of the display task’s turns is VSYNC, when the frame routine reads the keyboard. Right after that read, and a check that the key is not bouncing, comes this code in DisplayFrame:

; $0255: in DisplayFrame, after the keyboard read: the key exit
    ld hl,$403B      ; HL = CDFLAG
    res 0,(hl)       ; no new key yet
    jr nz,$0264      ; the reading changed, or is still bouncing
    bit 7,(hl)       ; steady: SLOW mode running?
    set 0,(hl)       ; CDFLAG bit 0: a new, steady key reading
    ret z            ; FAST mode: return to the key wait with it

RES 0 clears the bit first: no new key yet. If the reading has changed, or is still bouncing, JR NZ skips the rest. Once the same reading has stayed steady, SET 0,(HL) sets bit 0. In SLOW mode BIT 7 finds SLOW mode running, so RET Z is not taken and the frame carries on: VSYNC ends, and at the top border BorderLines hands the CPU back to the program task. The loop resumes exactly where it was stopped, with its own registers restored, so its HL still points at CDFLAG. Its next BIT 0,(HL) finds the bit set, and the key wait goes on to handle the key.

In FAST mode the same lines also end the frame routine’s call (“Two ways out” below), so the CALL Z comes back only once a key has arrived, and the loop’s first test succeeds at once.

Drawing while waiting

Called this way, DisplayFrame runs exactly as it does in SLOW mode, except that BorderLines sends both borders to FastBorder (Part 6). Its JP $0229 at the end keeps it going, frame after frame, with the display interrupt timing every line. Nothing else runs meanwhile: the ROM has nothing to do until a key arrives. There is no task switch and nothing saved, and IX is set and used within each border, never held across your program. That is why Part 2 lists IX and AF′ as free in FAST mode.

Two ways out

The frame routine has two RETs that only matter in FAST mode. The first is at its very start:

; $0229: the start of DisplayFrame: FRAMES, and the PAUSE exit
DisplayFrame:
    ld hl,($4034)    ; HL = FRAMES ...
    dec hl           ; ... counted down every frame
    ld a,$7F
    and h
    or l             ; have its lower 15 bits run out?
    ld a,h
    jr nz,FrCount    ; no
    rla              ; yes: bit 15 into carry, and cleared
    jr FrStore
FrCount:
    ld b,(hl)        ; only for the timing
    scf              ; carry set: carry on
FrStore:
    ld h,a
    ld ($4034),hl    ; FRAMES = HL
    ret nc           ; carry clear: a PAUSE ran out, return

Counting down.

    ld hl,($4034)    ; HL = FRAMES ...
    dec hl           ; ... counted down every frame

Every frame starts by counting the system variable FRAMES down by one. Its bit 15 is normally set; PAUSE is the one user that clears it.

Has it run out?

    ld a,$7F
    and h
    or l             ; have its lower 15 bits run out?
    ld a,h
    jr nz,FrCount    ; no
    rla              ; yes: bit 15 into carry, and cleared
    jr FrStore
FrCount:
    ld b,(hl)        ; only for the timing
    scf              ; carry set: carry on

AND H with $7F, then OR L, gives 0 only when the lower 15 bits of the count are all 0. While they are not, the routine goes to FrCount, where SCF sets carry: carry on. When they have run out, RLA moves bit 15 into carry instead (and clears it in the count). The two paths take exactly the same time, 23 T-states each: LD B,(HL) reads a byte nobody needs, just to make the shorter path as long as the other. PAUSE uses this same code: it puts its count, with bit 15 clear, in HL and enters at LD A,$7F.

The exit.

FrStore:
    ld h,a
    ld ($4034),hl    ; FRAMES = HL
    ret nc           ; carry clear: a PAUSE ran out, return

So carry comes out clear only when the lower 15 bits have run out and bit 15 was clear: that is, when a PAUSE count has run out. Then RET NC returns, and the PAUSE is over. In normal running, bit 15 is set, carry is set, and the frame carries on.

The second exit is in the key code you met under “The wait”, right after bit 0 of CDFLAG is set:

    bit 7,(hl)       ; steady: SLOW mode running?
    set 0,(hl)       ; CDFLAG bit 0: a new, steady key reading
    ret z            ; FAST mode: return to the key wait with it

In SLOW mode RET Z is not taken, as you saw. In FAST mode BIT 7 finds SLOW mode not running, and RET Z returns, with the new key, to the key wait.

That return has a visible side effect. It comes after the keyboard read, whose IN started VSYNC, and before the frame’s OUT ($FF) that would have ended it. So DisplayFrame returns with VSYNC still on, and the screen goes blank the moment the ROM accepts a key. It stays blank while the ROM handles the key, until the key wait calls DisplayFrame again and the next frame’s OUT ends the VSYNC. On Klive, one key press at the BASIC prompt blanked the screen for about 0.2 seconds. This is the famous FAST-mode flicker on every key press.

While a program runs in FAST mode

The rest of the time, your program (or the BASIC interpreter running it) has the whole CPU: no NMIs, no display interrupts, no display code at all. That is what makes FAST mode nearly 4 times faster (nearly 6 on an NTSC machine).

Why does the screen go blank while a BASIC program runs in FAST mode, rather than just freezing? The answer is VSYNC, which gets stuck on. As Wilf Rigter describes the ZX81 video hardware , an IN from port $FE pulls the video output down to the sync level and so starts VSYNC, but only while the NMI generator is off. While VSYNC is on, the ULA also stops making HSYNC, and only an OUT ends both. Now, between statements, the BASIC interpreter checks the BREAK key (SPACE) with the ROM’s routine at $0F46, which reads the keyboard with IN A,($FE) and never follows it with an OUT. In SLOW mode that IN is harmless, because the NMI generator is on. In FAST mode it is off, so the first BREAK check starts VSYNC and nothing ends it. The television receives a flat sync level, with neither HSYNC nor VSYNC to lock onto, and shows a blank screen until the program stops and the ROM draws frames again. What a real set made of that “blank” was usually noise. Klive’s emulated screen is black by default; Settings › Emulator › Show TV noise without sync draws the noise instead. It changes only the display, never the machine or its picture.

Rules for your programs

Sharing one CPU with the display comes with a few rules for machine code. They follow from everything above, so each one now comes with its reason.

Registers

Because the Z80 draws the picture, some of its registers belong to the display, not to your program. The display code relies on them even while your program is running:

RegisterThe ruleWhyWhere explained
IKeep $1E.The ULA takes the address of the character set from I ($1E00). With another value the screen shows the wrong shapes. Some high-resolution programs change it on purpose, for exactly this reason.Part 4: every opcode fetch
IYKeep $4000, always.The ROM reaches every system variable as (IY+n). In SLOW mode the border routine reads MARGIN and CDFLAG through IY while your program is running, so IY must be right at every moment, not just when you call the ROM.Part 6: entering the border
IXDo not change it in SLOW mode.It holds the frame routine’s bookmark: the last border NMI jumps through it with JP (IX).Part 6: entering the border, leaving it
AF′ (A′ and F′)Do not touch it in SLOW mode.A′ is the counter of border lines. Every NMI swaps it in with EX AF,AF' and counts it up, and your own EX AF,AF' would swap it away from the NMIs.Part 6: counting the lines
HL′Restore it before your USR code returns.USR is an operation of the ROM’s calculator, which keeps its place in HL′ and carries on from there when your code returns.—
InterruptsNo EI, unless you set up the display’s line loop on purpose (see below); keep interrupt mode 1.With interrupts on, the A6 trick fires an interrupt as soon as R’s bit 6 is clear during a refresh, which in ordinary code happens constantly, and the display’s interrupt routine runs with whatever is in your registers. The ROM selects IM 1, so that the display’s interrupt goes to $0038.Part 5: the A6 interrupt, why no EI
SPKeep some free stack below SP.In SLOW mode, the NMIs and the display code push onto your stack: your PC and four registers, plus a few return addresses on top.One stack for both

What is free: AF, BC, DE and HL, of course. So are BC′ and DE′, though ROM routines you call may change them. R is free too: reading it is a popular way to get a random number, and the display reloads it before every line. In FAST mode, IX and AF′ are free as well: there are no NMIs, and the border routine sets IX itself whenever the ROM shows a frame.

About EI. “No EI” really means “no EI unless you know exactly what will happen”. With interrupt mode 1, every accepted interrupt lands in the ROM’s line routine at $0038. That routine treats B, C, A and HL as its line counters and the address of a line, and jumps to HL. So interrupts are only safe with the CPU set up exactly as that routine expects. The ROM shows how: call DisplayLines ($02B5) with B, C, A and HL set up as Part 5 describes for the start of the text. The loop then runs your lines, and when B reaches 0 its RET Z returns to the instruction after your CALL, with interrupts off again. Klive confirms it: a FAST-mode program that called DisplayLines for one line got back exactly one interrupt later, with interrupts switched off. (In SLOW mode, do not try it: the border NMIs keep arriving while your program runs, and they would arrive in the middle of your lines.)

Hi-res graphics programs break two of these rules on purpose: they change I and IX to take over the display. Part 9 shows how.

Ports

Two of the ULA’s port rules matter while SLOW mode runs:

  • Reading the keyboard is safe. Your program only runs while the NMI generator is on, and then an IN from port $FE only reads the key rows; it does not touch VSYNC. (This is why BASIC’s own BREAK check, which reads port $FE between statements, does no harm in SLOW mode.) Often you do not even need to read the port: the display task reads the whole keyboard every frame and leaves the result in the system variable LAST_K ($4025).
  • Writing to a port can stop the display. On output the ULA looks at address lines A0 and A1 only, and an OUT to any port with A1 low, such as OUT ($FD),A, switches the NMI generator off. Then the border NMIs stop, the display task never gets the CPU back, and the picture is gone. An OUT to a port with A0 low switches the generator on.

Klive’s emulator shows both. A machine-code loop that keeps reading port $FE in SLOW mode leaves the frame exactly as it was: the same NMIs, the same display interrupts, the same 311-line frames. A single OUT ($FD),A stops every NMI and every display interrupt, and the emulated television falls back on its flywheel, with no picture.

The display file

The ULA’s bit 6 rule from Part 4 (steal and draw the bytes with bit 6 clear, let the others through as real instructions) has a trap for programs that write the display file themselves. The ROM’s PRINT only ever puts character codes and NEWLINEs in the display file. But nothing stops your own program from writing there directly, with POKE or with machine code. If it writes a byte with bit 6 set (anything other than $76), the ULA does not steal it. The CPU executes it as a real instruction, right in the middle of the display code, with the display code’s registers. What happens depends on the instruction. Three examples, tried on Klive’s emulator by poking a byte into the first line of the screen:

  • Harmless: $40 is LD B,B, which changes nothing. The line keeps its exact timing, and the position simply shows no character, because the ULA only draws the bytes it steals.
  • The picture breaks: $78 is LD A,B. It overwrites A, which holds the $DD that the display code loads into R before every line (Part 5 explains why). With R loaded wrongly, the interrupt that ends a line comes at the wrong moment. Some lines measured only 71 T-states instead of 207, and the picture falls apart.
  • The machine crashes: $C7 is RST 0, a jump to $0000, the power-on address. But the display code had just enabled interrupts, and the start-up code never disables them, so stray display interrupts keep hijacking the restart. In the test run the machine tumbled through more than 300,000 of them before it happened to restart cleanly, with the program gone.

Other bytes with bit 6 set are just as dangerous. The $C0–$FF range is full of jumps, calls, returns and restarts that leave the display file for good. $CB, $DD, $ED and $FD are prefixes that swallow the next character codes as part of a longer instruction. And the LD instructions in $40–$7F can overwrite A, B, C, H or L, which the display code uses to time its lines, count them and find them. So write only character codes into the display file, and leave its NEWLINEs exactly where they are: an extra $76 would end a line early and start one the ROM does not count.

Part 8: The keyboard, in constant time

Step 1 of every frame reads the keyboard, and on the ZX81 that is part of the picture: the routine’s first IN starts VSYNC, and VSYNC lasts until the frame routine’s OUT ($FF). So the keyboard routine sits inside the TV’s sync pulse, and that puts a strict demand on it: it must take exactly the same time every frame, whatever keys are down. If reading a pressed key took longer, VSYNC would grow with every key press, the top border would start at a different moment, and the picture could jump.

How the keys are wired

The 40 keys are wired as a grid of 8 rows of 5 keys. You read a row with IN from port $FE, and the high byte of the port address chooses the row: a 0 bit in it selects that row. So IN A,(C) with BC = $FEFE reads the row of SHIFT, Z, X, C and V; with B = $FD the next row; and so on up to B = $7F. Bits 0–4 of the result are the row’s five keys, 0 for a key that is down. (Bit 6 is the TV standard, which comes up again at the end of the routine, and bit 7 is the tape input.)

The routine

Here is the ROM’s keyboard routine at $02BB. It reads all 8 rows and returns HL, with a 0 bit for every row (in L) and every column (in H) that has a key down:

; $02BB: read the whole keyboard into HL (0 bits: keys down)
Keyboard:
    ld hl,$FFFF       ; no keys yet
    ld bc,$FEFE       ; B = $FE: the first row; C = the port
    in a,(c)          ; read the row (this IN starts VSYNC)
    or $01            ; first row only: leave SHIFT out
KbRow:
