    or $E0            ; bits 5-7 are not keys
    ld d,a            ; D = this row's keys, 0 = down
    cpl               ; now 1 = down: A = 0 when no key is down
    cp $01            ; carry when A = 0: no key in this row
    sbc a,a           ; A = $FF for no key, $00 for a key
    or b              ; A = $FF, or B: a 0 bit at this row's place
    and l
    ld l,a            ; L: a 0 bit for each row with a key down
    ld a,h
    and d
    ld h,a            ; H: a 0 bit for each column with a key down
    rlc b             ; the next row; no carry after the eighth
    in a,(c)          ; read it
    jr c,KbRow        ; always eight rows, whatever is pressed
    rra               ; carry = SHIFT (row $FE again, bit 0)
    rl h              ; H = the columns, shifted up, SHIFT in bit 0
    rla
    rla
    rla               ; carry = bit 6 of the port: the TV standard
    sbc a,a
    and $18
    add a,$1F         ; A = 55 (PAL) or 31 (NTSC)
    ld ($4028),a      ; ... into MARGIN
    ret

No decisions, only arithmetic

Look for the place where the routine decides “is a key down in this row?”. A beginner would write it with a jump:

    cpl
    and $1F           ; 1 bits: the keys down in this row
    jr z,NoKey        ; 12 T-states when taken, 7 when not
    ld a,b            ; a key is down: mark this row in L
    and l
    ld l,a
NoKey:

and the routine’s timing would then depend on the keys: a row with a key down would take longer than an empty one. The ROM never jumps on a key. It turns the answer into a mask instead, with these lines from the routine:

    cpl               ; now 1 = down: A = 0 when no key is down
    cp $01            ; carry when A = 0: no key in this row
    sbc a,a           ; A = $FF for no key, $00 for a key
    or b              ; A = $FF, or B: a 0 bit at this row's place
    and l
    ld l,a            ; L: a 0 bit for each row with a key down
  1. CPL makes the down keys 1s, so A is 0 exactly when no key in the row is down.
  2. CP $01 sets carry exactly when A is 0, because only 0 is below 1.
  3. SBC A,A subtracts A from itself with the carry: the result is $FF when carry was set (no key) and $00 when it was clear (a key).
  4. OR B then gives $FF (no key: changes nothing) or B, whose single 0 bit marks this row. AND L collects it into L.

Every row runs exactly the same instructions. The only jump is the loop’s JR C:

    rlc b             ; the next row; no carry after the eighth
    in a,(c)          ; read it
    jr c,KbRow        ; always eight rows, whatever is pressed

It depends on B, not on the keys: RLC B moves B’s single 0 bit to the next row, and carry stays set until all eight rows are done. So the jump is taken 7 times and falls through once, every time.

The end of the routine uses the same mask trick once more:

    rla               ; carry = bit 6 of the port: the TV standard
    sbc a,a
    and $18
    add a,$1F         ; A = 55 (PAL) or 31 (NTSC)
    ld ($4028),a      ; ... into MARGIN

SBC A,A turns bit 6 of the port into $FF or $00 again, and AND $18 and ADD A,$1F make that 55 or 31: the number of border lines, MARGIN, for a PAL or an NTSC machine. So the ZX81 checks which TV standard it is on 50 times a second.

Adding it up:

PartT-states
CALL $02BB17
LD HL, LD BC, IN, OR39
7 rows with the loop jump taken: 7 × (70 + 12)574
The 8th row, the loop jump not taken: 70 + 777
The end, from RRA to RET65
Total772

Klive’s core agrees: timed on the emulator, CALL $02BB takes 772 T-states with no key down, with one key, with keys in several rows, and with nine keys at once.

The frame routine around it follows the same discipline. Where it does have to choose (counting FRAMES down for PAUSE, and debouncing the key), it pads the shorter path until both take the same time. One path even reads memory into a register it does not need (LD B,(HL)), just to spend the same 7 T-states as the other path. Measured from the CALL $02BB to the end of the OUT ($FF), the whole of VSYNC takes 1,281 T-states, every frame, whatever you type.

Part 9: High-resolution graphics

The ROM’s picture is text: 64 shapes from the character set, in a 32 × 24 grid. A ZX81 has no bitmap screen at all. And yet ZX81 programs show full 256 × 192 pictures. The way they do it falls out of one detail of Part 4.

The detail: RAM sees the CPU’s own refresh address

During a NOP’s refresh cycle the CPU puts I × 256 + R on the address bus, and the ULA replaces the lower 9 bits with character code × 8 + line to point into the character set. But the ULA only does that for the ROM. The RAM is wired straight to the CPU’s address bus, so it sees the CPU’s own refresh address, I × 256 + R, unchanged.

So point I at RAM instead of the ROM (at $40–$7F on a 16K machine), and the byte that becomes the next 8 dots is simply the byte at address I × 256 + R. And R counts up by one with every NOP. Run 32 NOPs with I and R set up, and the ULA draws 32 consecutive bytes of RAM as one line of 256 dots: a bitmap.

This method is known as WRX, after Wilf Rigter, who developed it. Its display routine replaces the ROM’s text lines. Here is a complete one, written for this article and tested on Klive’s core:

HFile:  .equ $5000             ; the picture: 192 lines of 32 bytes
 
        .org $6800
HiRes:
        ld b,7
HrDelay:
        djnz HrDelay           ; a delay that puts the picture
        ld c,0                 ; 48 dots in from the left edge
        ld hl,HFile            ; HL = the first line's 32 bytes
        ld de,32               ; the length of a line
        ld b,192               ; 192 lines
        or b                   ; NZ, for the first line's RET NZ
HrLine:
        ld a,h
        ld i,a                 ; I = the line's address, high byte
        ld a,l                 ; A = its low byte, for R
        call LineRun+$8000     ; run the 32 NOPs in the RAM echo
        add hl,de              ; the next line's bytes
        dec b
        jp nz,HrLine
        call $0292             ; the bottom border: back to the program
        call $0220             ; VSYNC, keyboard, top border ...
        ld ix,HiRes            ; ... whose RET comes back here
        jp $02A4               ; back to the program, as BorderLines does
LineRun:
        ld r,a                 ; R = the low byte of the line's address
        .defs 32               ; 32 NOPs: each one draws the next byte
        ret nz                 ; 11 T-states: one more than RET
Start:
        ld ix,HiRes            ; USR Start: take over the bookmark
        ret

Every line by hand

There is no interrupt here: interrupts stay off, and nothing waits in HALT. The ULA keeps making HSYNC every 207 T-states from its own line timer, so the loop simply has to take exactly 207 T-states, every time round. Here is the loop:

HrLine:
        ld a,h
        ld i,a                 ; I = the line's address, high byte
        ld a,l                 ; A = its low byte, for R
        call LineRun+$8000     ; run the 32 NOPs in the RAM echo
        add hl,de              ; the next line's bytes
        dec b
        jp nz,HrLine

and the code it calls for each line, in the echo:

LineRun:
        ld r,a                 ; R = the low byte of the line's address
        .defs 32               ; 32 NOPs: each one draws the next byte
        ret nz                 ; 11 T-states: one more than RET

Adding them up:

InstructionT-states
LD A,H + LD I,A + LD A,L4 + 9 + 4 = 17
CALL LineRun+$800017
LD R,A9
32 NOPs128
RET NZ (taken)11
ADD HL,DE + DEC B + JP NZ11 + 4 + 10 = 25
One line207

Look at the RET NZ. A plain RET takes 10 T-states, and the line would be 206: one T-state short. A conditional return that is taken takes 11, which makes the line exactly 207. The condition is always true, because the flags still hold the result of DEC B from the line before, and B is not yet 0. That is also why the setup ends with OR B:

        ld b,192               ; 192 lines
        or b                   ; NZ, for the first line's RET NZ

It makes NZ true for the very first line, when no DEC B has run yet.

How much does one T-state matter? It is 2 dots. Klive shows exactly what happens with a plain RET: every line starts 2 dots further left than the one above, and the picture leans over and wraps round the screen. With RET NZ, every one of the 49,152 dots lands where the buffer says.

Two more details make it work:

  • R only counts in 7 bits. Its bit 7 never changes, so if a line’s 32 bytes crossed a 128-byte boundary, R would wrap round to the start of the block. Lines that start at a multiple of 32, as here, never cross one.
  • The NOPs run in the echo, at LineRun + $8000, just as the ROM runs the display file at D_FILE + $8000: the ULA only steals bytes fetched above 32K. LD R,A ($ED $4F) and RET NZ ($C0) both have bit 6 set, so they run as themselves.

Taking over the display

The routine plugs into the ROM’s frame through the IX bookmark from Part 6. In SLOW mode NmiLast ends with JP (IX), so a program only has to put its own routine in IX. That is all Start does:

Start:
        ld ix,HiRes            ; USR Start: take over the bookmark
        ret

The next time a top border ends, the ROM hands the text part of the frame to HiRes instead.

After its 192 lines, HiRes has to give the frame back without losing the bookmark:

        call $0292             ; the bottom border: back to the program
        call $0220             ; VSYNC, keyboard, top border ...
        ld ix,HiRes            ; ... whose RET comes back here
        jp $02A4               ; back to the program, as BorderLines does

Step by step:

  1. CALL $0292 runs the ROM’s bottom border. As always, BorderLines keeps the return address in IX and returns to your program, and the last border NMI comes back through IX to the instruction after the CALL.
  2. CALL $0220 enters the ROM in the middle of the routine that starts SLOW mode, at the instruction that pushes AF, BC, DE and HL. From there it falls into the frame routine: VSYNC, the keyboard, and CALL BorderLines for the top border. That BorderLines sets IX back to the ROM’s own bookmark, then pops the four registers just pushed and returns, not to your program, but to the instruction after CALL $0220.
  3. LD IX,HiRes takes the bookmark back, while the NMIs are already counting the top border.
  4. JP $02A4 jumps into the last part of BorderLines: POP HL … POP AF, RET. These pop the registers NmiLast saved, and return to your program, exactly as BorderLines would have.

So the ROM still does everything else: VSYNC, the borders, the keyboard. BASIC keeps running underneath and still reads its keys; only its text is no longer drawn.

Hi-res breaks two of the rules from Part 7 on purpose. It changes I, because pointing I at RAM is the whole idea, and it changes IX, because IX is how it takes over the display. A full screen needs 192 × 32 = 6,144 bytes of RAM, so it needs at least the 16K machine.

If the I register points into the ROM instead, the ULA does replace the lower address bits as usual, and the dots come from code × 8 + line in whatever 512-byte part of the ROM the I register selects. Changing I from line to line in this way gives what is often called “pseudo hi-res”: more shapes than the character set has, but still built from bytes that are already in the ROM.

Part 10: The 64K ZX81

On a 1K or 16K ZX81 the RAM appears twice in the address map, and the whole display trick depends on that echo: the ROM runs the display file at D_FILE + $8000 so that the ULA sees A15 high. On a machine with 64K, the upper 32K is not an echo any more but memory of its own. A jump to D_FILE + $8000 would run whatever happens to be stored up there, and there would be no picture.

RAM packs that keep the picture working solve this with one rule: an opcode fetch above $8000 is answered from the lower 32K. Data reads and writes see all 64K normally. So the display file still runs through “its echo”, even though the upper 32K holds different data. Klive’s 64K model works this way:

Address1K / 16K ZX8164K ZX81 in Klive
$0000–$1FFFROMROM
$2000–$3FFFthe ROM again (a mirror)8K of RAM
$4000–$7FFFRAMRAM
$8000–$FFFFthe RAM again (an echo)32K of RAM for data reads and writes; an opcode fetch here reads the RAM 32K lower

The 64K of RAM covers the whole address map, so its lowest 8K sits under the ROM. Data reads and writes at $0000–$1FFF reach the ROM, never that RAM. The only way to reach it is an opcode fetch at $8000–$9FFF, which the echo rule sends 32K lower. Everything else lines up with what the display needs: the display file is in the lower 32K, and its “echo” leads back to it.

What this means for programs:

  • The upper 32K is for data only. Your program can read and write any byte from $8000 to $FFFF as usual, but code stored there cannot run. If the CPU jumps there, every opcode fetch is answered from the RAM 32K lower, so the CPU never sees the code you put up there. It executes whatever lies at $0000–$7FFF instead, and the ULA’s bit 6 rule turns most of that into NOPs anyway. A hardware modification known as “M1NOT” lets code run in part of the upper 32K; Klive does not model it.
  • Machine code belongs below $8000. The 8K at $2000–$3FFF is ordinary RAM that code can run in, and so is any free memory in $4000–$7FFF. Use the upper 32K for what code works on: tables, pictures and buffers.
  • BASIC still lives below $8000. At power-on the ROM looks for RAM only from $4000 up to $7FFF, so RAMTOP is $8000 on the 64K machine, just as on a 16K one. BASIC never uses the 8K at $2000 or the upper 32K; they are there for machine code and its data.

Part 11: How Klive follows the beam

Klive’s ZX81 emulator does what the hardware does, at the level of single T-states. Its core is written in C, compiled to WebAssembly, and shares the Z80 with Klive’s other machines. The ULA hooks into that Z80 at a few well-defined points:

Hardware behaviourWhat the emulator does
The ULA’s line timerEvery T-state the Z80 spends advances a counter that wraps at 207. At T-state 16 HSYNC starts (the line counter goes up, and an NMI is raised if the generator is on); at T-state 32 it ends and the beam starts a new line.
Stealing a display byteOn an opcode fetch above $8000 of a byte with bit 6 clear, the memory read keeps the byte and returns $00.
Fetching the dotsAt each refresh, if a byte was kept, the core reads the character row from (I & $FE) × 256 + code × 8 + line counter and paints 8 dots at the beam’s current position.
INT on A6At each refresh with A6 low, an interrupt is raised for the end of that instruction. Acknowledging it resets the line timer.
WAITWhile the NMI line is active and the CPU is not halted, memory and port accesses take extra T-states until HSYNC ends.
VSYNCAn IN from an even port starts it, but only while the NMI generator is off; any OUT ends it and resets the line counter. While VSYNC is on, the core paints the picture black. Its line timer keeps counting underneath, where the real ULA stops making HSYNC, but none of that can show, so the screen looks the same.

The virtual beam is just two numbers:

  • x = 2 × (T-states since the last HSYNC ended): 2 dots per T-state.
  • y = the number of lines since the last frame ended.

The core paints into a raw 416 × 400 raster as the beam moves. A VSYNC at least one line long ends the frame (once the frame has 200 lines, the least a television would accept), and the core copies the visible 352 × 288 window out of the raster: the 256 × 192 picture with a 48-dot border on every side (352 × 240 on the NTSC model). If no VSYNC ever comes, which is what happens in FAST mode or after a crash, the core imitates the television’s flywheel and ends the frame on its own after 390 lines (328 on NTSC), just as a real set would roll on without sync.

Why the emulator cannot take a shortcut

It would be much simpler, and faster, to read the display file 50 times a second and draw 24 lines of text. Plenty of ZX81 software would break:

  • High-resolution graphics. Programs and games replace the ROM’s display routine with their own, point I at a table in RAM, or arrange their own NOPs, HALTs and R values, to draw pictures the character set could never produce (Part 9). They work only if the emulator does what the ULA does with each bus cycle.
  • Timing effects. A program that changes the display file while the beam is halfway down the screen shows the change from that line on.
  • Debugging. Because the display file really is executed, Klive’s tools see it that way: code coverage marks the display file as executed, and the execution history shows each line’s run of stolen bytes as forced NOPs.

Where to read the code

If you want to see the real thing, the ZX81 core lives in src/emu/machines/zx8081/wasm/ of the Klive repository. Its README.md maps every ULA behaviour onto the Z80 hook that implements it, and:

  • zx8081/zx8081-memory.c steals display bytes and puts NOPs on the bus;
  • zx8081/zx8081-ula.c holds the line timer, HSYNC, the NMI generator, WAIT, the A6 interrupt and the character fetch;
  • zx8081/zx8081-video.c is the virtual beam and the television: sync, flywheels and the visible window.

The ULA logic is ported from Thomas Harte’s Clock Signal emulator (MIT licence).

The display routines at a glance

Here are all the routines that make the picture, side by side, roughly in the order they run in a frame. The names are this article’s own; the addresses are the ROM’s.

RoutineAddressWhen it runsIts jobListed in
DisplayFrame$0229Once per frame. In SLOW mode always; in FAST mode only while the ROM waits for a key or a PAUSE.The conductor. Counts FRAMES, makes VSYNC around the keyboard read, then calls the top border, the text and the bottom border, and starts again.The frame routine
Keyboard$02BBOnce per frame, called by DisplayFrame.Reads the 8 key rows in a constant 772 T-states. Its first IN starts VSYNC. Also sets MARGIN from the TV standard.Part 8
BorderLines$0292Twice per frame: top and bottom border.Starts a border and keeps the frame’s place in IX. In SLOW mode it sets A′ to 1 − MARGIN, switches the NMIs on and returns into your program; in FAST mode it goes on to FastBorder.Entering the border
Nmi (the NMI handler)$0066At every HSYNC while the NMI generator is on: each border line in SLOW mode.Counts the border line in A′ and returns to your program straight away.Counting the lines
NmiLast$006FAt the last line of each SLOW-mode border.Saves your program’s registers, sets HL to the display file, HALTs for one more NMI to start in sync, switches the NMIs off, and jumps back into the frame through IX.Leaving the border
DisplayLines$02B5At the start of the text, and of each FAST-mode border.Starts the line loop: loads R for the first line, leaves $DD in A, enables interrupts and jumps into the display file.Entering the border
The display fileD_FILE + $8000Once per scan line of text.Not a routine anyone wrote, but code all the same: each character runs as a NOP that the ULA draws, and the NEWLINE runs as a HALT that waits for the interrupt.Part 4
IntDisplay (the INT handler)$0038At the end of every scan line of the text and of the FAST-mode borders.The line loop. Counts scan lines in C and text lines in B, runs the same line again or moves to the next, and reloads R with $DD. Leaves through RET Z after the last line.Running a line
FastBorder$02A9Each border in FAST mode.Draws MARGIN blank lines by running an empty display-file line through the line loop, then jumps back into the frame through IX.Entering the border
Stopping SLOW mode$02E7Whenever the ROM needs every T-state for itself: before SAVE, LOAD and printing.Waits for the next border NMI and switches the NMI generator off. The display loop is never resumed; it is simply abandoned.Starting and stopping the loop
Starting SLOW mode$0207At start-up, after the SLOW command, and whenever the ROM has paused the display for its own work: at the end of SAVE, LOAD and printing, and when it stops with an error report.Checks that the hardware produces display NMIs, saves your registers as NmiLast does, and enters DisplayFrame for the first time.Starting and stopping the loop

Summary

QuestionAnswer
Who reads the screen memory?The Z80, by jumping into the display file at D_FILE + $8000 and “executing” it.
Why doesn’t the CPU run the characters as code?The ULA replaces every byte with bit 6 clear by NOP and keeps the byte for itself.
Where do the dots come from?During each NOP’s refresh cycle the ULA reads one row of the character’s shape from the ROM at $1E00.
Why does a character take 8 dots?A NOP takes 4 T-states, and the ULA draws 2 dots per T-state.
What ends a line?The $76 at its end, a real HALT; R counts on to $80, A6 goes low, and INT fires after exactly 207 T-states.
How is each text line drawn 8 times?The ROM’s interrupt routine reruns the line 8 times; the ULA’s line counter picks the row of the shapes.
How do your program and the display share the CPU?In SLOW mode as two tasks: an NMI takes the CPU from your program at the end of each border, and a RET gives it back at the start of the next. In FAST mode the display is a subroutine, called only while the ROM waits for a key.
When does a program run?In SLOW mode, only in the top and bottom borders, between NMIs that count the blank lines. In FAST mode always, without a picture.
Why is the picture rock-steady?The ROM waits in HALT for the last border NMI, and the ULA’s WAIT holds the CPU to the end of HSYNC.
Why does reading the keyboard always take 772 T-states?It runs inside VSYNC, so it never jumps on a key: masks made with CP and SBC A,A replace the decisions.
How can a ZX81 show a bitmap?RAM sees the CPU’s own refresh address I × 256 + R, so with I pointing at RAM, 32 NOPs draw 32 bytes of RAM. A hand-timed 207 T-state loop, hooked in through IX, draws 192 such lines.
How does the display survive 64K of RAM?Opcode fetches above $8000 are answered from the RAM 32K lower, so the display file’s “echo” still leads back to it.
